title: Number of Laser Beams in a Bank
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every device pair directly versus a single-pass running product over consecutive non-empty rows.

content.title: Number of Laser Beams in a Bank

blocks.text: Given a 2D grid bank of '0's and '1's representing a bank's security devices, a laser beam connects two devices if they are on two DIFFERENT rows and there are NO devices in any row strictly between them. Return the total number of laser beams in the bank.

blocks.caption: Multiply the device counts of consecutive non-empty rows to count every beam between them

blocks.text: Given a grid representing security devices, count every laser beam, where a beam connects two devices on different rows only if no row strictly between them contains any device at all.

blocks.title: Analogy: Wiring Every Light on One Floor to Every Light on the Next Occupied Floor
blocks.text: Like wiring a laser tripwire security system across floors of a building, where lights on one floor are wired to every light on the NEXT floor that actually has any lights installed (completely skipping over floors with no lights at all, as if they don't exist for wiring purposes). The number of wires between any two such consecutive "lit" floors is simply the number of lights on the first floor multiplied by the number of lights on the second.

blocks.caption: Every device on one non-empty row connects to every device on the next non-empty row

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Row 0 has 3 devices. Row 1 is empty (skipped entirely). Row 2 has 2 devices: 3 * 2 = 6 beams","Beams so far: 6","Row 1 being empty means row 0 and row 2 are treated as consecutive for beam purposes"],["Row 3 has 1 device: 2 * 1 = 2 more beams","Beams so far: 6 + 2 = 8","Row 2 and row 3 are consecutive non-empty rows"],["Answer","8","Total beams: 6 (rows 0-2) + 2 (rows 2-3) = 8"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Only 1 non-empty row exists (row 1, with 3 devices)","No pair of non-empty rows exists","A beam requires TWO different non-empty rows; only one exists here"],["Answer","0","No beams can form with only a single non-empty row"]]}

blocks.text: Before checking every possible pair of devices directly and verifying nothing lies between their rows, notice that only consecutive NON-EMPTY rows ever matter, and the beam count between them is a simple multiplication.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A completely empty row (all zeros) contributes no devices, so it can never be an endpoint of a beam; more importantly, it doesn't BLOCK a beam either, since the "no devices in between" condition is trivially satisfied by an empty row.

Observation 2: This means the meaningful structure of the problem is really just the SEQUENCE of non-empty rows, with all-empty rows removed entirely from consideration.

Observation 3: Between any two CONSECUTIVE non-empty rows (in this reduced sequence), every device in the first connects to every device in the second, since nothing blocks any such pairing; the number of such beams is exactly (count of devices in the first row) times (count of devices in the second row).

Observation 4: Summing this product across every consecutive pair of non-empty rows, in a single pass tracking only the PREVIOUS non-empty row's device count, gives the total beam count directly.

Recognizing that empty rows can simply be skipped (rather than explicitly checked for "no devices in between") is what collapses an apparently pairwise device-counting problem into a simple running-product accumulation.
This is a running-value accumulation pattern: track only the previous non-empty row's device count, multiplying it against each new non-empty row's count and skipping empty rows entirely.
Find every individual device's position, then check every pair of devices on different rows to see if any row between them contains another device.

items: Record the (row, column) position of every device in the grid.
For every pair of devices on different rows (checked in a fixed row order to avoid double-counting), verify that no row strictly between them contains any device; if so, count this pair as a beam.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every individual device position is recorded first, since the brute force needs to check pairs of specific devices, not just row-level counts.
The r1 < r2 check ensures each pair is only ever counted once, in a single fixed order.
The "no device in between" check scans every row strictly between the two devices' rows directly.

blocks.text: Every pair of devices is checked directly against the beam-forming condition, so the correct total is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(d squared * rows) in the worst case, where d is the total device count, since every pair of devices might require scanning up to "rows" rows in between.
Space: O(d) for storing every device's position.

Limitation: checking every individual pair of devices, and re-scanning rows in between for each pair, ignores that only the device COUNT per non-empty row matters, and that the beam count between two consecutive non-empty rows is always simply their counts multiplied together.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every pair of devices individually. Instead, make a single pass over the rows, counting the number of devices in each row. Whenever a NON-EMPTY row is found, multiply its device count by the device count of the most recently seen non-empty row (tracked in a single running variable), adding this product to the running total, then update that running variable to the current row's count. Completely empty rows are simply skipped, neither contributing to nor resetting the running "previous non-empty count".

Maintain prevCount, initialized to 0. For each row, count its devices. If the count is greater than 0, add prevCount * count to the running total, then update prevCount to this row's count. If the count is 0, skip the row entirely, leaving prevCount unchanged.
Make a single pass, multiplying each non-empty row's device count against the previous non-empty row's count.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The running total after processing every row is 8, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), a single pass counting devices in every row.
Space: O(1) extra, using only a single running variable.

An empty row can never block a beam (since "no devices in between" is trivially true when the rows in between are themselves empty), so treating the sequence of non-empty rows as if they were directly consecutive is exactly correct. Between any two such consecutive non-empty rows, every device in the earlier row genuinely connects to every device in the later row (nothing in between blocks any of these specific pairings), so the beam count is exactly the product of their device counts, and summing this across every consecutive non-empty pair gives the true total.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Current row has at least 1 device","Add prevCount * (this row's count) to the total, then update prevCount"],["Current row has 0 devices (completely empty)","Skip entirely; prevCount remains unchanged, effectively treating this row as if it didn't exist"]]}

items: prevCount starts at 0, correctly contributing nothing until the FIRST non-empty row is encountered (0 * anything = 0).
Only non-empty rows ever update prevCount, ensuring the running value always reflects the most recent NON-EMPTY row's device count.
The single running total accumulates every consecutive pair's beam count directly, with no need for nested loops over device positions.

blocks.text: Recognizing that empty rows can simply be skipped (rather than explicitly verified as "nothing in between"), and that the beam count between two non-empty rows reduces to a simple product of their device counts, turns an apparently pairwise counting problem into a single running-value accumulation.

items: Explicitly checking every row in between for emptiness, instead of recognizing that simply skipping empty rows achieves the same effect automatically.
Forgetting to reset (update) the running previous-count value after processing a non-empty row, causing incorrect multiplications for subsequent rows.
Confusing "count of devices in a row" with "count of non-empty rows"; the running value must be the DEVICE count, not just 1 per non-empty row.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["bank has only 1 non-empty row","The answer is 0, since a beam requires two different non-empty rows"],["bank has no devices at all","The answer is 0, since prevCount and every row's count both stay 0"],["Every row has exactly 1 device","The answer is simply (number of rows - 1), since each consecutive pair contributes exactly 1 * 1 = 1 beam"]]}

items: Explicitly state why empty rows can just be skipped (rather than checked), since this exact realization is the key simplification that turns the problem from pairwise counting into simple running multiplication.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Count connections between elements across rows, but only between the nearest non-empty rows" points toward skipping empty rows entirely and tracking a single running "previous non-empty count", multiplying consecutive counts together.

items: How would you also report the actual device pairs forming each beam? Track the exact positions of devices in the previous and current non-empty rows, and generate the full cross-product of pairs explicitly (though this reintroduces O(d) space and output size).

What if beams needed at least 2 empty rows in between, not just "no devices"? This would require actually checking the empty-row-count between qualifying rows, reintroducing a more explicit row-by-row scan rather than a simple skip.

How would this generalize to a 3D grid (multiple floors of security devices)? The same running-product idea could extend along one additional axis, though the exact "consecutive non-empty layer" semantics would need careful redefinition.

A running-value accumulation pattern, conceptually similar to Kadane's Algorithm's single running value, but here tracking "device count of the previous non-empty row" and accumulating a PRODUCT rather than a sum or maximum.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(d squared * rows) time, O(d) space.
Optimized (running product over non-empty rows): O(rows * cols) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Single-pass running value accumulation, skipping empty rows and multiplying consecutive non-empty rows' device counts
Core Idea: Empty rows can simply be skipped (never blocking or counting); the beam count between two consecutive non-empty rows is exactly their device counts multiplied
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: An empty row trivially satisfies "no devices in between", so it can simply be skipped rather than explicitly checked
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Sum prevCount * currentCount across every non-empty row, skipping empty ones
